A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same VLM cue-bias and steering study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM evaluations, encoder comparisons, confidence analyses, and visual and language steering experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds frequency-conflict evaluations, training-stage comparisons, and further analyses of model responses.

M1.justification: The VQA and caption-extraction procedures, handcrafted and synonym prompts, and LLM-guided prompt optimization remain unchanged. Applying the existing steering procedure to frequency-conflict stimuli does not introduce a new algorithm or model component.

E1.justification: v2 adds an evaluated frequency-cue-conflict dataset of 1,200 images combining conflicting low- and high-frequency information (Section 5.2, Appendix G). This substantially extends coverage beyond texture/shape conflicts while retaining the original VQA and captioning tasks.

E2.justification: The main VLM, CLIP, and ImageNet comparator sets are retained. However, v1 Figure 5 compares visual steering against zero-shot and ImageNet-finetuned CLIP, whereas the corresponding v2 Figure 8 reports only LLaVA measurements; those experiment-specific comparisons are removed.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain stable. Added experiments introduce LF-bias evaluation on grayscale, spectrally blended images and a Stage 1 versus Stage 2 LLaVA checkpoint control. Confidence analysis expands from one to three models, and the prompt-search analysis includes LLaVA-NeXT 13B. These are targeted extensions of the retained evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds a training-stage ablation (Appendix M), agreement and error examples across 19 models (Appendix I), and prompt-search accuracy-versus-bias analysis (Appendix E). Confidence distributions extend to two additional models, and visual steering gains cue-specific accuracy analysis. Conversely, v1 Figure 3's correct-prediction confidence panel and confidence-threshold analysis are removed. Together these substantially revise the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v2 introduces two-sided t-test significance reporting at p < 0.05 for encoder shape-bias differences and frequency steering (Tables 1 and 2). The temperature experiment's three-seed reporting and stated single-seed exceptions are unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: The main benchmark scores remain unchanged, but substantial new results appear: frequency steering spans 32.9-38.6% LF bias for InternVL-Chat 1.1 and 48.7-54.5% for LLaVA-NeXT 7B, alongside training-stage and agreement-set results. Encoder-table model assignments are corrected: for example, LLaVA v1.5 7B's shape-bias delta changes from +4.2 to +1.5 percentage points. The reported maximum encoder error consistency changes from 79.8% to 78.7%.

T1.justification: The cue-accuracy and shape-bias equations are unchanged. v2 explains the already-used error-consistency metric through Cohen's kappa, but introduces no new formal assumptions, theoretical results, or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims that VLM biases differ from their encoders and can be steered through language remain intact. v2 explicitly extends steerability beyond texture/shape to frequency bias and elevates LLM cue suppression into a stated contribution. Its abstract foregrounds the limited effectiveness of shape-directed steering relative to texture-directed steering.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the training-stage ablation as evidence that instruction tuning encourages single-cue decisions and increases texture bias in the tested model. Appendix F newly distinguishes genuine steering from extreme corruption that destroys a cue. It also qualifies the generalizability of cue-conflict accuracy and makes the attribution of cue suppression to LLM processing more explicit.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproducibility statement reporting access to study code, per-sample model answers, searched prompts, the frequency dataset, and its creation scripts. Appendix G documents grayscale conversion, resizing, cropping, spectral blending, and JPEG settings. This substantially expands reproducibility information beyond v1's existing prompts and model descriptions.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Cohen on agreement, Oliva et al. on hybrid images, Geirhos et al. on shortcut learning, and Gavrikov and Keuper on generalization. It removes the no-free-lunch references and the earlier conclusion's CLIP prompt-engineering references. The central positioning within VLM and shape-bias research remains recognizable.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, and the abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Method descriptions and mechanistic analysis are reorganized; visual steering, several model observations, and other-bias discussion move into appendices. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 replaces confidence panels, redesigns the visual-steering plot, annotates language-steering accuracies, and expands the encoder table with significance markers and error consistency. It adds frequency and training-stage tables plus prompt-search, dataset-example, and agreement-set figures. Existing heatmap and class-wise plots are retained but relocated within a substantially reformatted document.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support and reproducibility: the frequency benchmark tests steering beyond the original cue conflict, the training-stage ablation probes its mechanism, and accuracy plots expose steering tradeoffs. Corrected encoder-table assignments and reported access to code, outputs, and dataset scripts address concrete reporting weaknesses. Some confidence diagnostics and visual-steering comparator results are lost, and stronger mechanistic interpretations remain partly indirect, but these costs are outweighed by the improved evidence and reproducibility.
